To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Mexican migrant men living in the United States have a high level of mental distress and that this distress is strongly associated with the stress of being separated from family members in Mexico.
46 % (46 %) of Mexican migrant men on the migration frontier in a new settlement in the Rocky Mountains of the United States had depressive symptoms in the clinical range.

46 % (61/134) of Mexican migrant men living in the Rocky Mountain Region reported depressive symptoms in a range for clinical concern; single and married men were at greater risk for poor mental health; and best predictors of depression included family separation and sending remittances, fearfulness, worry about confrontation with police, treatment by non-latinos and lack of support.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mental health of migrant men and the role of family separations in relation to depressive symptomology.
the mental health of a population that has been historically understudied and under-served, Mexican migrant men.
the mental health of migrant men in a rapidly changing region of the Rocky Mountain West.

the results of this study suggest that family separation and other stressors are associated with depression among Mexican migrant men on the migration frontier.
the study findings indicate that the mental health of the Mexican migrant men is poor and is related to both structural stressors and situational stress.
family separation, fearfulness, and other situational stressors are important predictors of depression among Mexican migrant men on the migration frontier.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the men we interviewed were very vulnerable to depression and that the best predictors were family separation and situational stress.
we need to understand the mental health of men who are separated from their families.
the mental health of these men is a complex issue that involves multiple stressors and protective factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mental health of migrant men in this new settlement is a public health issue and that it is critical to develop interventions that are culturally and contextually appropriate.
family separation is an important predictor of depression among Mexican men on the migration frontier, and that the impact of separation is exacerbated for men who are married and have children.
mental health interventions need to be complex and contextually sensitive, and they need to be designed to protect this population from stressors and promote their mental health.   1
